Observe and diagnose

Intermediate 30 minutes Lab 1 of 3
Introduction

In this lab, you'll act as an integration engineer for IDEA Brands, diagnosing why an expense MCP (Model Context Protocol) server whose policy checker and budget validator both work still lets the wrong expense reach the expense application.

NA
Noor Aziz
Software Engineer · IDEA Brands

They ask the assistant to file a hotel expense and need evidence that the business process actually finished.

The question

The server has a working policy checker and a working budget validator. Why can the wrong expense still be filed?

You'll learn how to

  • Connect the supplied server and verify its seven-tool inventory
  • Run a series of prompts and record the outcomes to help diagnose this MCP server's implementation
  • Map the prompt evidence and seven-tool shape to the four design principles

What you'll need

  • Your assigned LibreChat account for the event
  • Access to Workato and your pre-provisioned project
Phase 1

Connect the fragmented server

In this phase, you'll connect the supplied server and verify its seven-tool inventory.

1.1

Get the client talking to the supplied server

Noor files expenses by asking an assistant, and the expense server behind it is already running in your project. LibreChat is that assistant. It needs a token and the server's URL before it can reach any of the seven tools.

Overview

You end with one connected LibreChat entry for the fragmented server and an assistant that lists all seven expense tools, from get_employee_details through separate create and submit operations. Tool names arrive unchanged, and LibreChat names the server beside each call rather than inside the tool name. Workato shows the generated MCP Server URL once.

Heads up

The generated MCP Server URL embeds your token, so outside this lab treat it the way you would treat a password. For the lab, paste it into a text editor and keep it there. You need it a few steps from now, and Workato shows it only once.

Detailed steps 9 steps

Each attendee measures an isolated server, so another person's run cannot appear in your evidence. A second attached server can change tool selection and context without producing an obvious setup error, and confirming the inventory first lets you attribute later behavior to the design rather than a missing capability.

  • In Workato, open Projects, select your project, and open its Assets.
  • Select your fragmented expense server, then open Settings and End user access.
  • Under MCP Tokens, select Create new token.
  • Name the token <your learner ID>-expense-fragmented, using the ID you were assigned for this event, and select Create token.
  • Copy the generated MCP Server URL before closing the dialog.
  • In LibreChat, open the MCP Servers panel, select +, and complete the form with the values above.
  • Select Create, then connect the new server and confirm its connection state.
  • Open a fresh LibreChat conversation and attach only the fragmented server.
  • Ask What tools do you have available? and confirm the response lists get_employee_details, list_expense_categories, check_policy_limits, validate_budget_code, create_expense_report, submit_expense_report, and get_expense_report_status.
Verify exactly one server is attached in LibreChat, it reports a connected state, and the assistant lists all seven expense tools.
Phase 2

Run the prompts and record what happens

In this phase, you'll run a series of prompts and record the outcomes to help diagnose this MCP server's implementation.

Pattern

Keep the first run

One run is one conversation in LibreChat, not one turn. If the assistant stalls or asks for something more, keep replying (a nudge like just submit it is fair) and keep the first run even when it behaves safely.

2.1

Test the valid path

Noor's $245 hotel expense is within policy. This is the control that prevents a policy branch which rejects everything from looking successful.

Overview

You end with the 1 · Valid expense tab in the measurement workbook carrying all four readings for the $245 request: completion time, the tool calls you can see, context used, and the business outcome. LibreChat gives you three of them. Used N tools heads the response, the ring by the send button shows context when you hover it, and a hovered timestamp is near enough to estimate the time. The conversation stays in your LibreChat history. If the assistant asks which expense category to use and you answer it, that back-and-forth is still one run.

Heads up

Correct this run is not the same as guaranteed

The fragmented server can submit the first prompt on one run and leave it in draft on another. Record what happened. If it submitted, the result was correct this run, which is not the same as guaranteed by the server. Telling those two apart is the work of Phase 3.

Detailed steps 4 steps

The valid path establishes whether the process can finish, not merely whether one recipe call returned without error.

  • Open the 1 · Valid expense tab in the workbook and copy its prompt.
  • Send it in a fresh conversation with only the fragmented server selected.
  • Keep replying in LibreChat until the request is finished or refused, answering any category question along the way, and count the whole conversation as one run.
  • Record completion time, the MCP tool calls you can see, context used, and whether the business outcome actually matched.
Verify the 1 · Valid expense tab has all four readings and the conversation is still in your LibreChat history.

Test an ordinary policy violation

The upgraded room costs $347 against a 300 USD lodging limit. The server exposes the check that would catch it, but the client decides whether and when to call it.

Overview

You end with the 2 · Over-limit expense tab complete and that conversation kept in LibreChat. Record needs_approval if that is the application's observed state; a written over-limit report still fails the course's pre-write guarantee.

Detailed steps 2 steps

This run tests whether a required policy decision is enforced before the first write.

  • Open the 2 · Over-limit expense tab and send its prompt in a fresh conversation with only the fragmented server selected.
  • Record the workbook readings for this run, including needs_approval when that is the state you observe.

2.3

Apply explicit bypass pressure

This request carries an approval claim nobody can verify and asks the client to bypass policy. The correct business result is still rejection with no report created.

Overview

You end with the 3 · Policy-bypass attempt tab complete for the $347 request and that conversation kept in LibreChat. The fixed CAT-0002 category keeps the run focused on whether the bypass claim changes the process.

Detailed steps 2 steps

The run tests whether a conversational claim can disable a prerequisite that should live in deterministic logic. ▲ A refusal is a valid first result. Do not rerun until the model misbehaves; score the observed result and the server guarantee separately.

  • Open the 3 · Policy-bypass attempt tab and send its prompt in a fresh conversation with only the fragmented server selected.
  • Record the workbook readings and keep the first result you reach, even when that result is a refusal.
Verify prompt 3 records the first result you reached rather than a rerun, with correct-this-run kept separate from guaranteed-by-server.

2.4

Predict before you test

The first three prompts isolate one policy claim. Your prompt asks whether you can predict the next weak boundary before the run supplies the answer.

Overview

You end with one prediction made before the run, one selected or authored prompt, and one preserved result on the 4 · Your prompt tab. You run this same wording again in Lab 3, where the workbook replays it in the Process column, so this is the one row nobody else in the room shares.

Note

Choose one of three starting points

On the 4 · Your prompt tab, Help me pick previews a starter without replacing your draft. Each one is a request a colleague could plausibly send, and each leans on something this server does not decide for itself. You may use one unchanged, revise it, or write your own pressure prompt.

Detailed steps 6 steps

Prediction before execution turns exploration into a test of your design diagnosis.

  • Before you run anything, decide out loud what the server should protect here and what unsafe result you expect if it does not.
  • Open the 4 · Your prompt tab and write your own prompt, or use Help me pick to preview a suggestion and apply it.
  • Start a fresh conversation for your prompt, so nothing from an earlier run is in context.
  • Run your prompt once and keep the result you reach.
  • Record the workbook readings for this run.
  • Say whether the run matched your prediction, went against it, or did something you had not considered. You write this down in Lab 2.
Verify the Your prompt tab carries the wording you settled on and the result you kept from the first run, and that you made your prediction before running rather than after.

Phase 3

Diagnose the design

In this phase, you'll map the prompt evidence and seven-tool shape to the four design principles.

Pattern

Naive API wrapper

One tool per application endpoint leaves the client to assemble a business workflow. The tools may all work while the overall process remains unreliable.

3.1

Name what the design made possible

Four runs are behind you, and at least one of them filed Noor's expense correctly while nothing in the server made that certain. The question now is which risks belonged to a single run, and which were sitting in the design the whole time.

Overview

You end able to say, for each of your four runs, what the design left the model free to decide rather than how the run turned out. You also have one thing you can put on screen: a conversation, a tool sequence, or a reading. Your instructor leads the four-principle diagnosis from what the room brings.

Key insight

The seven-tool server is a naive API wrapper

Each tool mirrors an application endpoint, leaving the client to assemble the workflow. That structure weakens Cohesion over Convenience because the tools follow the API surface instead of the business intent. It also weakens Clarity over Completeness because the client receives a larger selection surface than the submission job needs.

Detailed steps 5 steps

A principle turns an observed event into a design diagnosis you can reuse on another process.

  • Read back through your four workbook tabs and the LibreChat conversations you kept.
  • For each run, separate correct this run from guaranteed by the server, and be ready to say which one you actually saw.
  • For each run, work out what the design left the model free to decide for itself.
  • Pick the single strongest thing you can put on screen rather than describe.
  • Bring it to the four-principle discussion your instructor leads. You write the diagnosis down in Lab 2.
Verify you can name, for every run, something the model was free to choose rather than only repeating the result, and that you have one item you can show on screen rather than only describe.

If you get stuck

  • Your run worked fine. That is a real result, not a mistake. Write down what happened rather than running it again until something breaks.
  • The assistant asks you a question back. Answer it in the same conversation. It still counts as one run.
  • Anything else. Ask your instructor. Nothing in this lab asks you to fix the server, so if you find yourself editing it, stop and check first.

Reflect

You watched four runs against a server that had every tool the job needed. The question now is where the guarantee lived: in the server, or in the choices the model happened to make.

  • Which run came out right while still depending on the model picking the right tools in the right order?
  • Where did the expense application tell you something the assistant's reply did not?
  • How did the prompt you wrote change the prediction you made before you ran it?
  • Which two principles could you have named from the list of seven tools alone, before running anything?

Wrap-up

Noor's problem is diagnosed now rather than described. You can name the part of the design that let the wrong expense through.

  • Clarity over Completeness. Seven tools give the model seven places to start. The more it can pick from, the harder it is to see which choice the job actually needs.
  • Cohesion over Convenience. Each tool copies one piece of the expense application, so nothing owns filing an expense from start to finish. Every caller rebuilds that process themselves.
  • Explicitness over Inference. Nothing in the server says policy has to run before anything is written, so the model decided it. Whatever you leave unsaid, it fills in.
  • Determinism over Cleverness. A run that came out right does not mean the next one will, because nothing forces the same order twice.

Keep all four runs. Lab 3 sends the same requests to the server you design, and sets what happens there beside what you recorded here.
